podcast.title: First Live US Appearance (1975)
podcast.body: During his first live performance in 1975 at the Paramount Theatre in Oakland, California, promoted by Bill Graham, Bob Marley's "bizarre appearance" in his street clothes and dreadlocks garnered a strong reaction from the audience. "Stephen said that the crowd, quote, gasped at the bizarre appearance of Marley in his street clothes and dreads and roared in approval when he whipped the dreads around."

podcast.title: Assassination Attempt (December 1976)
podcast.body: On the evening of December 3, 1976, around 8:30 PM, seven or eight armed men forcibly entered Bob Marley's house at 56 Hope Road outside of Kingston, Jamaica. Marley was shot twice, and his wife, manager, and a band employee also sustained gunshot wounds, though fortunately, no one died. The attack was reportedly orchestrated by elements within the Jamaican Labor Party (JLP) who perceived Marley as too politically progressive and influential, with some even suggesting CIA involvement. "Around 830 on the evening of December 3, 1976, 7 or 8 armed men burst into his house at 56 Hope Road outside of Kingston, Jamaica. Marley was shot twice."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Ed McCormick's Interview Impression (1976)
podcast.body: In a 1976 interview for Rolling Stone, Ed McCormick described encountering Bob Marley "whacked out of his skull" and in a state of "deep and herbal meditation" while smoking a spliff at his Hope Road house in Kingston. "In fact, Marley was so whacked out of his skull that it was possible to study him in perfect Nubian carving profile for several seconds before even dawned on him that he had company."

podcast.title: Acral Lentiginous Melanoma Diagnosis and Refusal of Amputation (July 1977)
podcast.body: In July 1977, a doctor in London diagnosed Bob Marley with acral lentiginous melanoma, a rare form of skin cancer discovered under his toenail that was not well documented in medical texts at the time. Despite the doctors' advice for toe amputation, Marley refused, citing his Rastafarian belief that removing any body part would be a sin, opting instead for a skin graft from his thigh performed by a Miami specialist. "In July, he visited a doctor in London, and they discovered he had something called Acro-leteginus melanoma, a pre-existing form of skin cancer under the nail that at the time wasn't well covered in the medical textbooks." "But Bob refused, saying that as a rastifarian, it would be a sin to have any body part removed."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Toe Injury Leading to Cancer (May 1977)
podcast.body: On May 9, 1977, in Paris, while playing soccer with bandmates between gigs, Bob Marley injured his big right toe when a French journalist wearing spikes stepped on it. This toe had been previously injured multiple times (by broken glass, a rock, almost cut off) and consistently struggled to heal, becoming a recurring issue. "One of the people he was playing with was a French journalist, and he was wearing spikes, and that guy stepped on Bob's foot. He injured his big right toe, and it didn't really seem to want to heal."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Central Park Collapse (September 1980)
podcast.body: Before his second show at Madison Square Garden on September 20, 1980, while running with his friend Alan Cole in Central Park, Bob Marley experienced altered vision, difficulty speaking, tightened legs, and searing neck pain, culminating in a multi-minute seizure and collapse. Despite this, he insisted on checking himself out of the hospital to perform the concert that night. "But before the second show, Bob went running with his friend Alan Cole in Central Park. His vision began to alter. He had trouble speaking. Suddenly his legs tightened, and he felt a searing pain in his neck. He collapsed and went into a seizure that lasted for several minutes."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Experimental Treatments with Dr. Joseph Issels (November 1980 - February 1981)
podcast.body: Discharged with only weeks to live, Bob Marley sought alternative treatments in Europe from Dr. Joseph Issels, a controversial figure described as a former Nazi who worked for Josef Mengele but resigned after refusing orders to stop treating Jewish patients. In Bavaria in November 1980, Marley, though weak, underwent Issels' experimental methods, including a special macrobiotic diet and drug-induced fevers using toxins to stimulate the immune system, along with the removal of decaying teeth and tonsils. By February 1981, after his 36th birthday, Issels attempted painful ozone injections into his navel, which only produced epileptic-like seizures and proved unsuccessful. "Through one of his Rastafarian contacts in Jamaica, he'd heard of a doctor named Joseph Isles, a former Nazi apparently, a guy who used to work for Joseph Mangalup." "Isles was offering some experimental cancer treatments."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Widespread Cancer and Unsuccessful Treatments (September 1980)
podcast.body: After collapsing in Central Park, Bob Marley reported back to the hospital on September 26, 1980, where doctors discovered that the melanoma had spread from his toe to his brain, forming a massive tumor, and also to his liver and lungs. He underwent chemotherapy and radiation treatments at Sloan Kettering Hospital, which caused his dreadlocks to fall out, leading to his wife giving him his first haircut in years. However, these conventional treatments proved ineffective. "doctors reported that the cancer had spread from his toe to his brain. There was a massive tumor. They also found cancer in his liver and lungs." "But the chemo and radiation did not work. There was nothing more they could do."

podcast.title: Death from Skin Cancer (1981)
podcast.body: Bob Marley's life was tragically cut short by skin cancer in 1981, though his passing did not diminish reggae's growing influence on global music. "Marley's death from Skin Cancer in 1981."

podcast.title: Death in Miami (May 1981)
podcast.body: On May 8, 1981, Bob Marley decided to return home to Jamaica and asked Chris Blackwell, head of Island Records, to fly him there. However, his vital signs worsened during the flight, forcing the plane to land in Miami, where he was taken to Cedars of Lebanon Hospital. Critically ill and in immense pain, he died on May 11, 1981, surrounded by his family and weighing only 82 pounds, at the age of 36. "He was critically ill and in a tremendous amount of pain. But there was nothing the doctors could do except offer large amounts of powerful pain killers. And then, surrounded by his family and weighing just 82 pounds, Bob Marley died. It was May 11, 1981."

podcast.title: Rock and Roll Hall of Fame Induction (1994)
podcast.body: Bob Marley was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1994, an event that was regarded as effectively inducting reggae itself and formally recognizing its profound historical importance in music. "There is a reason that he was inducted into the rock and roll hall of fame way back in 1994. It was like inducting reggae and acknowledging the historical importance of it."

podcast.title: "Rock Star" Marketing Strategy
podcast.body: Chris Blackwell intentionally positioned Bob Marley as a rock star, a strategic move made after acknowledging that Marley would not get airplay on black radio stations, aiming instead for mainstream rock exposure and further emphasized by his American booking agent, Don Wine-trop, who insisted on headline-only shows for Marley. "Chris Blackwell was going for. He told Marley he was not going to get played on black radio stations, so he was going to market him as a rock star."

podcast.title: BBC Archive Recordings (Multiple Years)
podcast.body: Bob Marley is among the numerous artists who contributed to the BBC's extensive archive of recordings. These sessions were often a way for artists to have their music broadcast on the BBC during periods when "Needle Time" restrictions limited the amount of commercially released music that could be played. "Even from the Beatles to Bob Barley to Joy Division to Tears for Fiers and literally thousands of other artists were invited to make records at the BBC so they could get around the whole Needle Time thing."

podcast.title: Birthplace and Mausoleum at Nine Miles
podcast.body: Bob Marley was born in Nine Miles, a village in St. Anne Parish, Jamaica, which is now entirely owned by the Marley family. His childhood home has been converted into a museum. Adjacent to the museum is a mausoleum where Bob Marley's remains are interred, along with a guitar he was buried with, the remains of his mother (who died in 2008), and his brother (who was killed in 1990). The site is a significant shrine for Jamaican culture and for fans globally. "The house where Bob grew up is out in the country, a place called Nine Miles in St. Anne Parish."

podcast.title: Bob Marley - Exporter of Jamaican Dreadlocks
podcast.body: Bob Marley is internationally celebrated as the leading figure who brought Jamaican-style dreadlocks to the world, making them a globally recognized and significant symbol. "The most famous exporter of Jamaican style dreads was of course Bob Marley."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Bob Marley's Hair Copied with Reggae's Global Spread
podcast.body: With the international expansion of reggae music in the mid-1970s, Bob Marley's distinctive dreadlocks hairstyle became widely imitated, and this trend has continued ever since. "When people began to export reggae to the world in the middle 1970s, people began to copy Bob Marley's hair and have been doing it ever since."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Bob Marley's Role in Dreadlocks Popularity in Music
podcast.body: Although Bob Marley did not originate dreadlocks, his influence was paramount in making them a prominent and integral part of the music scene, solidifying his role as an "exporter of reggae and dreadlocks to the world." "Well, Bob Marley did not invent the dreads, but he did make them a big deal in music."

podcast.title: Bullet Retention for Guitar Playing
podcast.body: Following the assassination attempt, a lead bullet remained lodged in Bob Marley's upper left arm. He chose not to have it removed, fearing that the removal surgery, due to its location, might cause damage that would make it difficult or impossible for him to play the guitar. "He could have had it removed, but he chose not to. Why? Well, because of its location, we're moving it might have caused damage that would have made it hard if not impossible to play the guitar, so it stayed."

podcast.title: Dreadlocks as Rastafarian Symbol of Lion of Judah
podcast.body: As a devoted Rastafarian, Bob Marley wore dreadlocks as a powerful religious symbol representing the Lion of Judah, a sacred emblem deeply rooted in Old Testament traditions. "He was a Rastafarian and dreads were a symbol of the lion of Judah, a religious symbol that stretches all the way back into the Old Testament."

podcast.title: Extensive Family
podcast.body: Bob Marley, often referred to as the "King of All Things reggae," had at least 12 children with seven different mothers, and potentially more. Many of his children have pursued their own musical careers. "Bob Marley. The King of All Things reggae had at least 12 children, 12 that we know of, with seven different mothers. There may be more, but we're not sure."

podcast.title: Influence on Alt Rock
podcast.body: Although Bob Marley is not categorized as an alternative artist himself, his music has exerted a significant and lasting influence on Alt Rock throughout several decades. "Not an alternative artist per se, but his music has had plenty of influence on Alt Rock through the decades, so it will be a crime to leave him out, so let's put Bob Marley on the list."

podcast.title: Influence on Bad Brains
podcast.body: Bad Brains were big fans of Bob Marley, which led them to incorporate Reggae into their sound. This blending of genres introduced Reggae to a new generation of listeners, showcasing Marley's lasting impact. "And because they were big Bob Marley fans, they also eventually incorporated Reggae into their sound, bringing that genre to a whole new generation of kids."

podcast.title: Influence on Skateboarding Culture
podcast.body: Bob Marley's music has been a significant influence on the sport and culture of skateboarding. There is even a documentary that explores the extent of his impact on the world. "Bob Marley's music was a big influence on skateboarding. There's even a documentary exploring his impact on the world."

podcast.title: Last Words to Son Ziggy
podcast.body: Bob Marley's final words, spoken to his son Ziggy while surrounded by family, were a poignant message of support and expectation: "on your way up, take me up. On your way down, don't let me down." "He said, on your way up, take me up. On your way down, don't let me down."

podcast.title: Les Paul Jr. and Reggae Sound
podcast.body: Bob Marley was a notable fan of Gibson's Les Paul guitars, particularly the Les Paul Jr., which he modified. The unique sound produced by this instrument, tailored to his specifications, played a crucial role in bringing reggae music to a global audience. "Bob Marley was a fan of the Les Paul guitars Gibson eventually started making. His main instrument was a Gibson Les Paul Jr. He modified it a bit, and the sound it produced brought reggae to the world."

podcast.body: Mount Zion Rock is identified as Bob Marley's favorite place to meditate. podcast.title: Parasitic Crustacean Species
podcast.body: In 2002, a tiny new crustacean was discovered in the Caribbean around the US Virgin Islands. This parasite, named *Genathia Marley-I* after Bob Marley, hides in sea sponges, algae, and dead coral, feeding solely on the blood of specific fish, with the French grunt fish being a favored host. "It was first found by a marine biologist named Paul Sickle. He gave it to a South African member of his research team named Nico Smith, who confirmed that this was a brand new species. And together, they decided on the name, Genathia Marley-I, after Bob, of course."

xref.title: Desmond Dekker – Jamaica's Top Singer of the 1960s; Ska's First Worldwide Hit (1969); Worked in Welding Shop with Bob Marley
xref.body: Desmond Dekker used to work in a Jamaican welding shop alongside a kid from St. Anne's parish named Bob Marley. Dekker became Jamaica's top singer of the 1960s and, thanks to Island Records (run by Englishman Chris Blackwell, who was in love with Caribbean music), scored ska's first worldwide hit in 1969. "He used to work in a Jamaican welding shop along a kid from St. Anne's parish named Bob Marley."

xref.title: SNL Pope John Paul II Photo Tear (October 3, 1992) – Career-Ending Television Moment
xref.body: After a series of controversies (refusing to appear on SNL while Andrew Dice Clay was host in 1990; refusing the national anthem before a New Jersey show in August 1990; skipping the 1991 Grammys despite four nominations; a perceived pro-Saddam comment in March 1991), Sinead O'Connor appeared on *Saturday Night Live* on October 3, 1992, singing Bob Marley's "War." In rehearsal she held a picture of a refugee child; live, she substituted a photo of Pope John Paul II — taken from her mother's bedroom wall — and tore it up at the word "evil," saying "fight the real enemy." There was complete silence from the studio audience. NBC received nearly 5,000 complaints and the resulting media blowback permanently ended her mainstream career. The inspiration was Bob Geldof tearing up a picture of John Travolta on *Top of the Pops* in the 1970s. "NBC received almost 5,000 complaints. The blowback in the media was intense and her career never, ever recovered."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Saturday Night Live Pope Photo Tearing (1992)
xref.body: On October 13, 1992, as a musical guest on *Saturday Night Live*, Sinead performed an a cappella version of Bob Marley's "War" instead of her scheduled second song. During the performance, she held up a picture of Pope John Paul II (found on her mother's wall after her death) and tore it to pieces, declaring, "Fight the real enemy." This act, which she stated was planned to destroy a symbol of "lies and liars and abuse" associated with the Catholic Church and her mother, generated immense controversy. "Instead, she held up her mom's picture of the Pope and tore it to pieces."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Saturday Night Live Pope Tearing (1992)
xref.body: On October 3, 1992, as the musical guest on *Saturday Night Live*, Sinéad O'Connor tore up a picture of Pope John Paul II during her a cappella performance of Bob Marley's "War." She did this at the exact moment she sang the word "evil," tossing the pieces towards the camera and saying, "Fight the real enemy," to protest child abuse in the Catholic Church. "But when the show went live, she held up a picture of Pope John Paul II, which she then proceeded to tear up as a way of protesting against child abuse within the Catholic Church."

xref.title: Camden Rehearsal Space
xref.body: The band rehearsed in a building in Camden, which notably featured a jukebox. This jukebox was stocked with the latest singles from contemporary bands like The Ramones, as well as reggae songs from Jamaican artists such as Bob Marley and dub pioneer Lee Scratch Perry. The Clash particularly favored Dub music, identifying it as the music of the immigrant communities with whom they shared their neighborhood. "The clash rehearsed in a building in Camden that featured a jukebox stock with the latest singles from bands like The Ramones and Reggae Songs from Jamaican artists like Bob Marley and Dub Pioneer Lee Scratch Perry."

xref.body: Ziggy Marley is Bob Marley's eldest son and has achieved significant musical success, winning five Grammy Awards. He also wrote the theme song for the children's TV show "Arthur" and published a comic book titled "Marijuana Man." "Ziggy is Bob's eldest son. He's won five Grammy Awards, wrote the theme song for the children's TV show Arthur, and published a comic book called Marijuana Man."

xref.title: Formation and Lineup

Their song "Tomorrow People" featured Ziggy, his mother Rita, and his sisters Sadella and Sharon, along with his brother Stephen. "The Melody Makers were formed by siblings David, better known as Ziggy, Steven, Sadella, and Sharon back in 1979."

"And because they were big Bob Marley fans, they also eventually incorporated reggae into their sound, bringing that genre to a whole new generation of kids."

xref.title: Genre Blending and Influence
xref.body: Being big Bob Marley fans, Bad Brains eventually incorporated Reggae into their sound, exposing the genre to a new generation of kids. Later, they further diversified their music by introducing elements of funk, soul, and even hip hop, making them hugely important on multiple levels. "And because they were big Bob Marley fans, they also eventually incorporated Reggae into their sound, bringing that genre to a whole new generation of kids. Later, funk and soul and even hip hop was introduced. Again, hugely important on so many levels."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Giant of Rock Music
xref.body: Ike & Tina Turner are recognized as significant figures in the broader landscape of rock music. "I can teen a turner, funk a delix, Stevie Wonder, Bob Marley, Prince or Slash."

xref.title: Inspiration for The Specials' Logo
xref.body: Peter Tosh, a Jamaican musician and former member of Bob Marley's Wailers, was the real-life individual whose photograph inspired the stylized Jamaican rude boy character, Walt Japsco, featured in The Specials' band logo. "Walt was actually based on a photograph of Jamaican musician Peter Tosh, who was a former member of Bob Arley's Whalers."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Marriage to Rohan Marley
xref.body: Lauren Hill, a singer, is married to Rohan Marley, the son of Bob Marley. "He's married to singer Lauren Hill."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Matriarch and Performer
xref.body: Rita Marley is the mother of several of Bob Marley's musical children and performed with the Melody Makers, including on their hit song "Tomorrow People." "It features Ziggy, Mother Rita, Sisters Sadella, and Sharon and Brother Stephen."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Museum Curator
xref.body: Sharon Marley is responsible for looking after the Bob Marley Museum located in Kingston. "Sharon looks after the Bob Marley Museum in Kingston."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Musical Influence (1970s)
xref.body: In her youth, Sinead O'Connor gravitated to the music of Bowie, along with Bob Marley, disco, early punk, and Barbara Streisand. "Later it was Bowie and Bob Marley and Disco in early punk, and Barbara Streisand."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.body: Barbara Streisand was among the artists whose music Sinead O'Connor gravitated towards in her youth, alongside Bowie, Bob Marley, disco, and early punk. "Later it was Bowie and Bob Marley and Disco in early punk, and Barbara Streisand."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Peter Tosh as Walt Japsco Inspiration
xref.body: The character Walt Japsco, central to The Specials' logo, was directly based on a photograph of the Jamaican musician Peter Tosh, a former member of Bob Marley's Wailers. "Walt was actually based on a photograph of Jamaican musician Peter Tosh, who was a former member of Bob Arley's Whalers."
